passage: Anand had worked out his speech while feeding the buffaloes. When his mother Disha came back from the well, he did not sulk about the mela as he had last year. "Ma, the evening aarti at the temple fair is at seven. Can I stay till the last bus at eight-thirty?" Disha kept wringing her dupatta. "Who else is going?" "Cousin Dev and two boys from school. I finished the fodder and I'll carry the phone. I'll call from the bus stand." She looked at him a long moment. "If you call, and you're back by nine, then yes. We'll see how it goes and talk again next time." Anand nodded, smiled, and did not push for more.

qa.q: Where was Anand when he prepared his request?
qa.a: He was feeding the buffaloes.

qa.q: What does Anand want from his mother, and what in his behaviour suggests it?
qa.a: He hopes to stay for the evening aarti at the mela and wants her trust, shown by his prepared speech and the reasons he gives. He is trying not to sulk as he did last year.

qa.q: What made Disha say yes?
qa.a: His respectful tone, the concrete details about who is going and when he will call, and the fact that he finished his chores made the request easier to trust.

qa.q: How might Disha feel as she agrees?
qa.a: She may feel a little worried, yet proud that he asked properly, so a trial for one evening feels reasonable. 🙂

grounding: A teen appeals to a parent with reasons and a respectful tone, and it works better than pressure.

passage:
In Uppsala, midsummer meant a party at Lina's lake house, and it would still be light at midnight. Rosa had been planning her pitch for three days.
She waited until her mum, Ulla, had finished her coffee.
"Can I ask you something properly?" Rosa said, sitting down. "Lina's party. I'd like to come home at one, not eleven."
Ulla raised an eyebrow. "Last year you said everyone else could stay out, so I should let you."
"I know. That was a bad argument." Rosa slid a paper across. "This is better. Lina's parents will be there. Anna's father drives us home at one. Here's his number. And I'll text you at eleven and at half past twelve."
Ulla read it twice, a small smile growing.
"Half past twelve," she said. "Anna's father, and both texts."
Rosa grinned. "Deal."

qa.q: Who would drive Rosa home after the party?
qa.a: Anna's father would drive them home at one.

qa.q: What was Rosa probably feeling as she slid the paper across?
qa.a: She was probably hopeful but nervous, since she had planned the pitch for three days and knew last year's argument had failed.

qa.q: Which choice of Rosa's worked, and why?
qa.a: Bringing facts in a calm, respectful way, such as the parents at the party, the ride home and the check-in texts, worked better than last year's "everyone else can" pressure.

qa.q: How does Ulla see this year's request compared with last year's?
qa.a: Ulla seems impressed and more trusting, because this time Rosa gave real reasons and a safety plan instead of pressure.

grounding: The scene shows a teenager appealing for a later curfew with respectful tone and evidence, which succeeds.

passage:
On the girls' hostel notice board, lights-out was ten, even in exam week. Two girls had already argued with the warden, Kashish Ma'am, in the corridor. One had shouted, "Then we'll all fail and it'll be your fault." The door had shut in their faces.
Ira tried something else. She collected signatures from twenty-two girls in Block B who wanted to study late. Then she knocked on the office door after dinner.
"Ma'am, may I ask about exam week?" She laid down the list. "We're asking for eleven-thirty, only in the common study hall, not in rooms. Two seniors will sign everyone out at the end. And we'll keep it silent so the juniors can sleep."
Kashish Ma'am read the list slowly. "Who are the two seniors?"
Ira named them.
"Try it for three nights. If the hall stays quiet, we'll continue."

qa.q: How many girls signed Ira's list?
qa.a: Twenty-two girls in Block B signed the list.

qa.q: What was Kashish Ma'am likely thinking as she read the list slowly?
qa.a: She was probably cautious but interested, weighing whether the plan was safe, and she may have felt respected after the shouting in the corridor.

qa.q: What made Ira's appeal succeed where the other girls failed?
qa.a: Ira asked politely, brought evidence of support, and offered a clear, safe plan, while the others used threats that made the warden shut the door.

qa.q: What is it like for Kashish Ma'am to be threatened in the corridor?
qa.a: It probably felt disrespectful and stressful, making her less willing to bend the rule for the girls who shouted.

grounding: The hostel scene shows a teenager appealing for a later lights-out with respectful tone and evidence, which works better than threats.

passage:
Subject: Meenu's sangeet - can I stay till the end?

Dear Papa,
I know you're on night shift this week, so I'm writing instead of asking at breakfast.
Meenu's sangeet is on Saturday. Last time I asked to stay late somewhere I sulked and said you never trust me. That was not a good way to ask, and I'm sorry.
So here are my reasons. Meenu is my closest friend and I'm dancing in two items, one of them near the end. Chachi will be there the whole night, and she has offered to drop me home by eleven-thirty with her own daughter. I'll call you when I leave the hall and when I reach home.
If eleven-thirty is too late, could we agree on eleven and I'll ask to dance earlier?
Please reply when you wake up.
Nirmala

qa.q: Who offered to drop Nirmala home by eleven-thirty?
qa.a: Chachi offered to drop her home by eleven-thirty with her own daughter.

qa.q: What does Nirmala's apology for sulking suggest about Nirmala's feelings?
qa.a: It suggests Nirmala feels a little ashamed of how the last request went and hopeful that a calmer, respectful request will be trusted more.

qa.q: What makes this email a good appeal?
qa.a: It is respectful, gives clear reasons and a safety plan, and offers a fair compromise of eleven, instead of pressuring Papa.

qa.q: How might Papa feel reading this after his night shift?
qa.a: He would probably feel reassured and respected, and more willing to agree because the email shows planning rather than sulking.

grounding: The email shows a teenager appealing to a parent for a later return with reasons, respect and a compromise.

passage: Okay Ojas, you asked how I got Appa to agree to eleven o'clock for the farewell, so here's the whole thing. First try, last week, total disaster. I stood in the kitchen and said, "Everyone else can stay till eleven, and if you say no I'll just go anyway." Appa didn't even look up from the dosa pan. "Then it's nine." Door closed. Second try, I waited till after dinner, when he was relaxed with the news on. I said, "Can I ask you something properly?" Then I showed him: the farewell ends at 10:30, Suresh's dad is driving four of us back, here's his number, and I'll message at 10:30 and again at the gate. I even said, "If I'm late once, you decide the next one." He called Suresh's dad right then. Eleven, done. So yes, this is me, Pradeep, the guy who finally learnt that threats lose and reasons win.

qa.q: Who is driving four of them back?
qa.a: Suresh's dad is driving four of them back.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling during the first try in the kitchen?
qa.a: Pradeep was likely frustrated and desperate not to miss out while everyone else could stay till eleven, which came out as the threat to go anyway. It may also have been embarrassment at having an earlier time.

qa.q: What made the second appeal work?
qa.a: Pradeep chose a calm moment, asked to talk properly, and brought facts: the end time, the driver's number, check-in messages and an offer to accept a consequence. 👍

qa.q: How might Appa have felt hearing the threat compared with the plan?
qa.a: The threat likely made Appa feel pushed and defied, so he shut it down; the plan gave him information and some control, so he could say yes.

grounding: It shows a teenager appealing to a parent for a later curfew, first with a threat that fails and then with reasons and a respectful tone that succeed.
